facts.title: model accuracy
facts.text: The fare model is a gradient boosted decision tree trained on log(base_fare). On the unseen test month it is off by $5.02 on a typical trip (mean absolute error) and explains 80.4% of the variation in fares (R-squared 0.804).
facts.keywords: how accurate good performance result score works well reliable trust error rate correct

facts.title: what MAE means
facts.text: Mean absolute error is the average size of the model's mistake, ignoring whether it guessed high or low. $5.02 against a typical fare of about $19 is roughly 26% out.
facts.keywords: mean absolute error metric measure evaluate

facts.title: what R-squared means
facts.text: R-squared is how much of the variation in fares the model explains. Always guessing the average fare scores 0, a perfect model scores 1, and a model worse than the average scores below 0.
facts.keywords: r2 r squared metric measure evaluate variance explained

facts.title: why baselines are shown
facts.text: The simple baselines are published next to the model on purpose. A model that cannot beat a straight line through distance is not worth shipping, and an R-squared on its own says nothing about whether the score was hard to reach. The gap between the straight line and the full model is the part worth claiming.

facts.title: the price range
facts.text: The range shown around each estimate comes from two more models trained with quantile loss at the 10th and 90th percentile, not from a rule of thumb. 79.5% of real fares land inside that band against a target of 80%, so the uncertainty is calibrated. The band is $16.69 wide on average.
facts.keywords: confidence interval uncertainty band prediction interval quantile how sure certainty

facts.title: train and test split
facts.text: The model trains on 2025-09, 2025-12, 2026-01 and is tested on 2026-04, a later month it never saw. The split is by month and never random: a random split lets the model see the future and reports a score it could not repeat in use. It learned from 5,851,185 trips and was scored on 1,969,989.
facts.keywords: validation overfitting leakage cross validation holdout evaluate how tested

facts.title: features the model uses
facts.text: The model is given twelve features: pick-up zone, drop-off zone, trip miles, hour, day of week, whether it is a weekend, whether it is a public holiday, whether it is a holiday eve, whether the provider is Uber, whether the ride was requested as shared, and whether either end is an airport.

facts.title: data leakage
facts.text: Trip duration, tips, driver pay and price per mile are deliberately kept out of the model. All of them are only known once the ride is over, so feeding them in would leak the answer and produce a score the model could never repeat on a real request.
facts.keywords: leak cheating target leakage overfit

facts.title: what the model leans on most
facts.text: By permutation importance the model leans most on trip miles, which costs 1.441 of R-squared when shuffled. Then come pu zone (0.065), do zone (0.055), hour (0.038), is uber (0.009).
facts.keywords: feature importance which features matter signal driver influence

facts.title: how feature importance is measured
facts.text: Importance is measured by permutation: one feature's values are shuffled at random and the drop in accuracy is recorded. A feature that changes nothing when scrambled was not being used. This is measured on the test data rather than read off the trees, because a tree's built-in importance favours columns with more distinct values.

facts.title: zones matter beyond distance
facts.text: After distance, the pick-up and drop-off zones are the strongest signals. That is the model learning that the same mile costs different amounts in different parts of the city, which a plain distance formula cannot do.

facts.title: how distance is worked out
facts.text: The site only knows two zones, but the model needs miles. It uses the median distance actually driven between that pair of zones, measured over 22,470 pairs with enough trips. For a pair with too few trips it falls back to the straight-line distance multiplied by a detour factor of 1.3762, which was measured from the data rather than guessed: NYC streets make a trip about 38% longer than flying straight.
facts.keywords: miles km distance calculate route haversine detour

facts.title: why gradient boosted trees
facts.text: Gradient boosting builds many small decision trees one after another, each correcting what the ones before it got wrong. Trees were chosen because fares are not linear: airport trips are near flat rate and rush hour bites differently in each zone. A linear model needs those interactions written out by hand, and trees find them. They also handle zone ids naturally, train in minutes on a laptop with no GPU, and can be explained.

facts.title: why the log of the fare
facts.text: The model predicts the logarithm of the fare rather than the fare itself. Fares are right-skewed, with many small ones and a few very large ones. Training on the log makes the model minimise percentage error instead of dollar error, which is what matters to a rider, and it makes a negative prediction impossible.
facts.keywords: target transform skew logarithm transformation

facts.title: demand model result
facts.text: The demand side predicts pick-ups per zone per hour. The honest result is that the trained model lost. The lagged model wins outright, but it needs the last few hours of real counts and the site has no live feed. Without lags the model scored below the plain zone x hour x weekday average, so the site serves that lookup instead. The lagged score is reported to show what a live feed would buy; neither model is saved, because nothing loads them.

facts.title: weather was tested and dropped
facts.text: Weather was tested as a feature and rejected. Rain lifts the citywide mean fare 5-6% in September and April, but that lift is already carried by hour and zone, which the model has. The test here is whether weather adds anything on top. On the same rows and the same split, adding temperature, rainfall and wind moved the error from $5.080 to $5.089 and R-squared from 0.799 to 0.794 - very slightly worse. The weather columns are not used by the model.
facts.keywords: rain raining weather temperature failed experiment rejected negative result

facts.title: does rain raise fares
facts.text: Rain does lift the citywide mean fare by about 5-6% in September and April, and made no measurable difference in January. But hour and zone already carry that signal, so giving the model the weather on top added nothing.

facts.title: size of the dataset
facts.text: The project is built on 78,211,750 cleaned trips from New York City's Taxi and Limousine Commission High Volume For-Hire Vehicle records, covering 4 months: 2025-09, 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-04. They were chosen to cover autumn, the winter holidays, cold and rain.

facts.title: which companies
facts.text: The data covers Uber and Lyft. Uber is 72.7% of the trips read (56,893,909) and Lyft is 27.3% (21,317,841).

how the data was cleaned
facts.text: About 6.1 to 6.5% of raw rows are dropped per month, most of them trips with an unknown pick-up or drop-off zone. A trip is kept only if its distance is between 0.1 and 100.0 miles, its duration between 1 minute and 6 hours, its fare between $1 and $1000, its wait under 60 minutes, its price per mile between $1 and $100, and its average speed between 1 and 60 mph.
facts.keywords: cleaning preprocessing filter outliers removed dropped quality preparation

facts.title: why those cleaning limits
facts.text: The limits come from looking at the data, not from habit. The raw price per mile reaches $3,951 a mile, speeds run past anything a NYC street allows, and zones 264 and 265 mean unknown or outside the city and have no shape on the map.

facts.title: no feature scaling
facts.text: Values are kept in real units with no scaling or normalisation. Tree models do not need it, the site has to display $24.50 rather than 0.37, and a scaler must be fitted on the training split only, so it belongs inside a model pipeline rather than in the stored data.

facts.title: holidays in the data
facts.text: The model is told about public holidays and holiday eves. The holidays covered are Labor Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Day, Good Friday and Easter, plus Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve as eves.

facts.title: what this project is
facts.text: NYCRide is a fare prediction site for New York City. You pick a pick-up zone, a drop-off zone and a time, and it prices the trip, shows the range around that price, prices all 24 hours and all 7 days so you can see when to travel, compares Uber against Lyft on that exact route, and shows what the model gets right and wrong.
facts.keywords: about overview summary describe explain purpose goal nycride what does it do

facts.title: the point of the project
facts.text: The point is honesty about the model, not just the prediction. Every score on the site is read from the trained model's own metrics file rather than typed in, plain baselines are shown next to the model, and the two experiments that failed are reported alongside the ones that worked.
facts.keywords: why built motivation purpose interview portfolio

facts.title: what the site can tell you
facts.text: The site has seven sections: the estimated fare with its range and both providers, the best time to leave, cheaper pick-up points nearby, the same trip across the week, what single change would make it cheapest, the weather experiment, and a model lab with the scores and baselines.

facts.title: technology used
facts.text: Python with scikit-learn for the models, pandas and PyArrow for the data, FastAPI for the API, and plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for the maps. No frontend framework and no paid APIs.
facts.keywords: tech stack framework library tools languages built with python fastapi sklearn

facts.title: why NYC data and not India
facts.text: An Indian ride-hailing dataset was tried first and rejected. Profiling it showed the fare had almost no correlation with distance, the hourly patterns were flat and the counts were suspiciously round - it was synthetic, so no model trained on it would mean anything. No real Indian trip data of this kind is public, and NYC's TLC publishes real records, so the project moved to New York.
facts.keywords: india indian delhi synthetic fake kaggle dataset choice why new york

facts.title: how fast the site is
facts.text: A prediction takes about a millisecond. Nothing at request time touches the 78 million row data files: the models and the lookups are loaded once when the service starts, and every endpoint works from those.

facts.title: limitations: what the data cannot say
facts.text: The things that really move a fare - live traffic, the surge multiplier, the exact route taken and how many drivers are free - are not in the data at all, because a TLC record is written after the trip is over. That is the ceiling on accuracy here, and roughly $5 of error is close to it.
facts.keywords: weakness weaknesses problem problems drawback shortcoming limitation fail wrong bad improve better surge traffic

facts.title: limitations: coverage
facts.text: The project covers New York City only and four months only. There is no vehicle category, no passenger count, no surge column and no cancellation data in the source.
facts.keywords: weakness scope cities months coverage limitation

facts.title: limitations: events
facts.text: Street closure permits for parades and street festivals stop appearing in the city's event feed after 2016, so the 2025-26 months carry Parks Department permits only. Events are a weak signal and the all-zero column is dropped rather than fed to a model as noise.

facts.title: limitations: weather is one reading
facts.text: Weather is a single city-wide hourly reading, so local showers are missed. Visibility comes back empty from the archive and is dropped.

facts.title: why a group vehicle optimiser was dropped
facts.text: An earlier idea was to work out the cheapest mix of vehicles for a group - two cabs against two autos, say. It was dropped because New York has no auto-rickshaws or bike taxis, and the records carry no vehicle type at all, so the prices would have had to be invented.

facts.title: where the data comes from
facts.text: Trip records come from the NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission's High Volume For-Hire Vehicle monthly files. Zone shapes come from the TLC taxi zone shapefile, weather from the Open-Meteo archive, and the road routes drawn on the map from the public OSRM routing service.

facts.title: how the Ask feature works
facts.text: This answer comes from a retrieval system over facts built directly from the project's own metrics and data files. The question is matched against those facts, the closest ones are passed to a language model, and it writes the answer from them. Questions about the price of a specific trip are sent to the fare model itself instead, so the number is a real prediction rather than something retrieved.
